one_liner: Zero-copy C11 YAML 1.2 event parser and emitter with an SSE4.2 scanner; parses 1.6-13x faster than libyaml.
what_it_does: A pull-style YAML 1.2 parser. You call yam_parse_next() in a loop and get const yam_event pointers (stream/doc/mapping/sequence/scalar/alias) whose value/anchor/tag are (pointer, length) spans into your input buffer or an arena. It also has a lower-level token scanner, an event-driven emitter (block, flow and minimal styles) that writes to an in-memory buffer, opt-in merge-key and alias expansion, and pluggable tag schemas (failsafe/JSON/core/custom). The API is different from libyaml's (yam_* functions, arena ownership, no yaml_parser_t), and there is no DOM.
how_it_is_fast: The scanner looks for structural bytes 16 at a time with SSE4.2 PCMPESTRI range compares and SSE2 compare-and-movemask. The SSE4.2 or scalar version is chosen once through function pointers set in a load-time constructor. Plain and quoted scalars that have no escapes or line breaks come back as zero-copy slices of the input. Block scalars, and quoted scalars with escapes or line breaks, are copied into a bump-allocated arena a line or a run at a time, not byte by byte. The parser is an incremental state machine; to decide whether a flow collection is a key, it looks ahead with a SIMD bitmask over 64-byte windows and caches the answer for nested collections, which keeps it linear.
when_to_use: C or C++ code that walks YAML as an event stream (config loaders, CI and Kubernetes-style files, converters) and wants more throughput than libyaml's yaml_parser_parse.
Inputs dominated by long scalars: literal/folded block scalars and multi-line quoted strings measured 7-13x faster than libyaml, and 2-8x faster than rapidyaml's event parser.
JSON-like or compile_commands.json-style files that are already in memory (about 2.2 GB/s vs 226 MB/s for libyaml in the author's table).
You need strict YAML 1.2 conformance (all 308 valid and 94 invalid YAML Test Suite cases pass) plus a round-trip-safe emitter, on x86-64 Linux or macOS.
when_not_to_use: You want a document tree or DOM. yam only produces events, so you would build the tree yourself; libfyaml or rapidyaml give you one.

You need streaming input from a FILE*, a callback or a socket, or UTF-16/UTF-32 input. yam parses one contiguous UTF-8 buffer that has to stay alive, and emitter output goes to an in-memory buffer too.

The documents use anchors, tags, %TAG/%YAML directives, flow keys in block mappings, merge keys or alias resolution. Any of these makes the parser re-parse the whole stream in eager mode and buffer every event, so memory grows with the whole stream. The anchored 'config' benchmark shows the smallest gain (206 vs 125 MB/s, 1.65x).
Structure-heavy input with short keys and values, if C++ is an option: rapidyaml's event parser was 1.3-1.8x faster than yam on the generated block, mixed and JSON inputs.

You are risk-averse about maturity. The project was created in Feb 2026, has 0 stars and no external issues, and one maintainer. 1.0.0 is in the header and CHANGELOG, but the newest git tag is v0.3.1.

integration.form: static lib | shared lib (Makefile builds libyam.a and libyam.so.1 plus yam.pc; about 8 C files, easy to vendor)
integration.min_toolchain: C11 with GCC or Clang (uses __attribute__((constructor)), target("sse4.2") and __builtin_cpu_supports; POSIX headers); tested with GCC and Clang on Linux and macOS; MSVC/Windows not documented
integration.platforms: x86-64 uses SSE4.2 when the CPU has it, with a scalar fallback chosen at runtime, so no -march=native is needed. There is no NEON path, so aarch64 and other non-x86 targets run the scalar code. CI covers Linux and macOS.
integration.thread_safety: not documented. From the source: all state is per parser/scanner/emitter/arena, schema presets are static const, and the only global is the SIMD function-pointer table, which is set once at load time. So separate parsers on separate threads look safe, but a single parser or arena is not synchronized.

gotchas: The parser stops with YAM_ERR_LIMIT after 10,000 events by default. The README says that is roughly 100-200 KB of dense YAML, and the author's benchmark sets it to 0. Call yam_parser_set_max_events() for large files.
An event pointer is valid only until the next yam_parse_next() call. The value/anchor/tag spans are not NUL-terminated and stay valid only while both the input buffer and the arena are alive.

It is stricter than libyaml, which implements YAML 1.1. Tabs as indentation, implicit keys spanning lines and similar input are errors. Schemas are opt-in, so scalars carry no resolved tag unless you set one. There is one deliberate leniency: a closing ] } or quote may sit at any indentation.

Eager mode (tags, anchors, merge or alias expansion) parses recursively at roughly 1 KB of stack per nesting level. If you raise max_depth or set it to 0 (default 256), deep input can overflow the stack.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick yam over libyaml or libfyaml when you want a plain C event API and more throughput: 1.6-3.4x on structure-heavy YAML and up to 13x on long scalars, with the same full test-suite conformance as libfyaml. Pick rapidyaml or chyaml instead if you are in C++ and your input is mostly short keys and values or you want a tree; also consider yeptris if you target Apple Silicon, since yam's SIMD is x86-only.
verified_claims_summary: The author's make bench-compare harness parses the same ~10 MB inputs (generated block/mixed/JSON/config YAML, rapidyaml's real travis.yml, appveyor.yml and compile_commands.json files, and scalar-heavy text) into events with yam, libyaml 0.2.5 and libfyaml 0.9.6. It ran on one pinned core of an Intel Core Ultra 7 155H, with yam built by GCC 16.2 at -O2 and the other two linked as system libraries. yam measured 1.65x (anchored config) to 13.4x (multi-line double-quoted) over libyaml, e.g. 501 vs 149 MB/s on travis.yml. This is first-party and not independently reproduced.
status_note: Actively developed by a single author (last commit 2026-09-24, 1.0.0 with an ABI-stability promise declared in the CHANGELOG), fuzzed on every push and daily through ClusterFuzzLite, and MIT-licensed. It is small enough to vendor, but it has no track record of outside users yet.
